sections: Welcome

Before a building goes up, someone digs, carries, levels, and cleans. That crew member is often a construction laborer.

This is physical, outdoor work on a team. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is a Construction Laborer?

You do the hands-on work that keeps a construction project moving. You help skilled workers, run small machines, and keep the site safe and clean.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Load and unload materials and carry them where they are needed.
  • Dig, shovel, and level ground and gravel.
  • Help pour and finish concrete.
  • Run tools like compactors, saws, and jackhammers.
  • Signal equipment operators and direct traffic around the site.
  • Clean up to remove hazards.

The real picture: The work changes with each job. Roads, houses, farms, and oil field sites all need laborers, and in North Dakota much of the work is busiest from spring through fall.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: Every crew and job site is different.

  • Early morning: Meet the crew, put on safety gear, and hear the plan for the day.
  • Morning: Unload a delivery of lumber and rebar and stack it where it goes.
  • Midday: Help set forms and spread gravel before a concrete pour.
  • Afternoon: Help finish the concrete and run a compactor.
  • Before leaving: Clean tools and pick up the site so it is safe overnight.

Weather changes plans. Some days start before sunrise to beat the heat, and some jobs pause when it storms.
How You Learn the Job

Most people learn on the job. Many employers hire people with a high school diploma or GED, and some do not require one. Read the actual job ad.

  • On-the-job training: An experienced worker shows you the tools and safety rules.
  • Apprenticeship: Some contractors and the Laborers’ union offer construction craft laborer apprenticeships, where you are paid while you learn.
  • Safety training: Many employers ask for or provide OSHA 10-hour safety training.
  • Optional classes: North Dakota schools offering construction trades programs include Turtle Mountain College in Belcourt and Sitting Bull College in Fort Yates. Compare cost, length, and schedule.

Paying for training: In an apprenticeship you are paid while you learn, and pay usually rises as you complete hours. For classes or a certificate, start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. Ask employers whether they help pay. Ask your career counselor about other help, such as WIOA, a federal program that can help some people pay for job training. Ask before you enroll.
Training and Employer Requirements

North Dakota does not license construction laborers. Building contractors need a state contractor license, but that is the employer’s job, not yours. Ask each employer what you need to start.

  • Ability to lift and carry heavy materials, or ask about the job’s physical demands.
  • Steel-toed boots and some basic gear; ask what the employer provides.
  • A driver’s license and reliable ride to job sites that move.
  • Safety training, which many employers provide.
  • Drug testing for some employers.

Before you begin: Ask who trains new workers and what safety gear you will be given.

Ask about written instructions, a buddy on your first jobs, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and work safely.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota construction laborer pay — May 2025:

  • Middle pay: $23.59 an hour ($49,070 a year). Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $21.96 and $29.17 an hour.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $18.75 an hour, and 1 in 10 earned more than $34.23.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 5,150 of these jobs in 2024. The state projects about 5,650 in 2034, a change of +10%. That works out to about 480 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

Where people work: Building contractors, road and bridge crews, oil field and energy projects, farms, and cities and counties.

Work setting: Outdoor job sites in all kinds of weather. Many jobs are full time in busy season, with early starts and some long days.

Compare an offer: Ask about base pay, overtime, winter work, travel pay, benefits, and what safety gear is provided.
Where This Can Lead

• Experienced laborer: Run more equipment and take on harder tasks.
  • A skilled trade: Many laborers move into carpentry, concrete finishing, pipe laying, or equipment operation.
  • Crew leader or foreman: Lead a crew as experience grows.
  • Construction manager: With experience and sometimes more school, plan and run whole projects.

Ask people on the crew which paths are open where you live.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • Seeing a project rise because of your work.
  • Working outside with a crew.
  • Starting without a degree and learning on the job.
  • Many paths into skilled trades.

Things to ask about:

  • Hard physical work that can be tough on your body over time.
  • Weather, including North Dakota winters.
  • Seasonal layoffs or long days in busy season.
  • Travel to job sites far from home.

North Dakota projects about 10% growth in these jobs from 2024 to 2034, with about 480 openings a year.

A question for yourself: Does physical work on a team, outside, sound like a good fit for you?

sections: Welcome

Pallets of food, parts, and supplies move through North Dakota warehouses every day. Forklift operators move them.

This job mixes careful driving, safety, and steady work. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is a Forklift Operator?

You drive a forklift or similar machine to load, move, and stack materials. You work in warehouses, factories, lumber yards, and shipping docks.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Inspect the forklift before each shift.
  • Load and unload trucks and rail cars.
  • Move pallets to the right shelf or work area.
  • Check labels and order numbers so the right load goes to the right place.
  • Watch for people and obstacles while driving.
  • Record what was moved, sometimes with a handheld scanner.

The real picture: Some jobs are mostly driving. In others, you also pick orders, wrap pallets, and help on the dock.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: Every warehouse runs on its own schedule.

  • Start of shift: Walk around the forklift and check tires, forks, horn, and brakes.
  • Morning: Unload two trucks and put pallets away on high racks.
  • Midday: Move materials to the production line as they are needed.
  • Afternoon: Load outgoing orders onto trucks in the right order.
  • End of shift: Park and charge or fuel the forklift and report any problems.

Busy days can feel fast. Safety always comes before speed.
How You Learn the Job

Most people learn on the job. Many employers hire people with a high school diploma or GED, and some do not require one.

  • Employer training: Federal safety rules require each operator to finish training and an evaluation before driving on their own. The training mixes classroom learning, hands-on practice, and a driving test at work.
  • Start nearby: A warehouse, stocker, or material mover job can lead to forklift work.
  • Refreshers: Operators are evaluated again at least every three years, or after an accident or near miss.

There is no state forklift license. A card from a class somewhere else does not replace your employer’s own training and evaluation, so ask before paying for a class.
Training and Employer Requirements

Requirements depend on the employer. Ask what you need to start.

  • Completion of the employer’s forklift training and evaluation.
  • Good eyesight, hearing, and attention to people nearby.
  • Ability to climb on and off the machine and sometimes lift boxes.
  • Willingness to work shifts, which may include nights or weekends.
  • Drug testing for some employers.

Before you begin: Ask who trains new operators and how much practice time you get.

Ask about written instructions, an accessible workstation, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and do the work well.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota forklift operator pay — May 2025:

  • Middle pay: $23.68 an hour ($49,260 a year). Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $21.65 and $27.07 an hour.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $19.58 an hour, and 1 in 10 earned more than $30.14.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 990 of these jobs in 2024. The state projects about 1,060 in 2034, a change of +7%. That works out to about 100 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

Where people work: Warehouses, distribution centers, factories, grain and farm supply businesses, lumber yards, and shipping companies.

Work setting: Usually indoors in a warehouse or plant, sometimes in outdoor yards. Shifts may include nights and weekends.

Compare an offer: Ask about base pay, shift pay, overtime, benefits, and how the employer trains and evaluates operators.
Where This Can Lead

• Experienced operator: Drive other equipment, such as reach trucks or loaders.
  • Lead or trainer: Train new operators and lead a shift.
  • Warehouse or shipping supervisor: Run a dock or a whole shift.
  • Truck driving: Some operators go on to earn a commercial driver’s license.

Ask your employer which paths are open.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • Running equipment instead of lifting everything by hand.
  • Clear tasks with a finish line each shift.
  • Starting without a degree.
  • Jobs in many industries.

Things to ask about:

  • Hot, cold, or noisy warehouses.
  • Night or weekend shifts.
  • Pressure to move fast.
  • The risk of accidents if safety rules are not followed.

North Dakota projects about 7% growth in these jobs from 2024 to 2034, with about 100 openings a year.

A question for yourself: Do careful, steady driving and safety rules sound like a good fit for you?

sections: Welcome

A leaky faucet, a broken door, a light that will not come on. Someone has to fix them, and in many buildings that person is the maintenance worker.

This job mixes many small trades. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is a Maintenance and Repair Worker?

You keep buildings, equipment, and grounds in working order. You do routine upkeep and fix problems as they come up.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Do routine upkeep, like changing filters, belts, and fluids.
  • Find out why something stopped working.
  • Repair doors, locks, fixtures, and drywall.
  • Do small plumbing and painting jobs.
  • Order parts and supplies.
  • Keep records of the work you finished.

The real picture: A school job, an apartment job, and a factory job are very different. Some work is mostly building repairs; some is mostly machines.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: Every building has its own list.

  • Morning: Check the work orders and plan the route.
  • Later: Replace a faucet part and fix a sticking door.
  • Midday: Change air filters in the heating system.
  • Afternoon: Answer an urgent call about a leak.
  • Before leaving: Write down what was finished and order a part for tomorrow.

Plans change when something urgent breaks. Some jobs include being on call.
How You Learn the Job

Many people learn on the job, often after a high school diploma or GED. Many employers like to see a certificate or experience in a trade.

  • On-the-job training: An experienced worker teaches the building’s systems.
  • Apprenticeship: Building and industrial maintenance apprenticeships pay you while you learn.
  • Short classes: Courses in HVAC, plumbing basics, or electrical safety can help you get hired.
  • Start nearby: Janitor, groundskeeper, or helper jobs can lead to maintenance work.

Paying for training:

  1. Start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. The school's financial aid office can help.
  2. Ask employers whether they help pay for training.
  3. Ask for the full cost, including books, fees, travel, and a computer.
  4. Ask your career counselor about other help, such as WIOA. WIOA is a federal program that can help some people pay for job training. Ask before you enroll.

Employer help with school may come with a promise to keep working there. Read the terms first.
Training and Employer Requirements

There is no general state license for maintenance work. Some tasks are licensed: in North Dakota, electrical wiring work needs a state electrical license, and plumbing has its own rules. Ask exactly what your job will include.

  • Comfort with hand and power tools.
  • Ability to climb ladders, lift, and work in tight spaces, or ask about the physical demands.
  • A driver’s license for jobs that cover several buildings.
  • A background check for jobs in schools or health care.

Before you begin: Ask which repairs you will do yourself and which go to licensed trades.

Ask about written instructions, a buddy on your first jobs, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and work safely.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota maintenance and repair worker pay — May 2025:

  • Middle pay: $23.96 an hour ($49,840 a year). Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $20.06 and $28.68 an hour.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $17.44 an hour, and 1 in 10 earned more than $32.91.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 3,680 of these jobs in 2024. The state projects about 3,980 in 2034, a change of +8%. That works out to about 380 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

Where people work: Schools, apartment buildings, hospitals and clinics, factories, hotels, and cities and counties.

Work setting: Inside and outside buildings, often moving from task to task. Some jobs include on-call or weekend duty.

Compare an offer: Ask about base pay, on-call pay, overtime, benefits, and whether the employer pays for classes.
Where This Can Lead

• Lead maintenance worker: Take on harder repairs and train others.
  • Facilities supervisor or manager: Run maintenance for a building or campus.
  • A licensed trade: Electrician, plumber, or HVAC technician through an apprenticeship.
  • Industrial maintenance: Specialize in factory machines.

Ask people where you work which paths are open.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • Fixing things and seeing them work again.
  • A different mix of tasks every day.
  • Jobs in almost every town.
  • Skills you can use at home, too.

Things to ask about:

  • On-call duty, nights, or weekend emergencies.
  • Dirty, cramped, or hot spaces.
  • Lifting and climbing.
  • Many people asking for help at once.

North Dakota projects about 8% growth in these jobs from 2024 to 2034, with about 380 openings a year.

sections: Welcome

Fresh paint changes how a room or building feels. Behind every clean edge is a painter who did careful prep work first.

This job mixes detail, patience, and physical work. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is a Painter?

You prepare and paint walls, ceilings, trim, and outside surfaces of homes and buildings.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Cover floors and furniture and tape off edges.
  • Fill cracks and holes, then sand and scrape.
  • Apply primer, paint, and stain with brushes, rollers, or sprayers.
  • Set up ladders and scaffolding safely.
  • Read work orders and match colors.
  • Clean up tools and the work area.

The real picture: Much of the job is preparation. Painting outside is seasonal in North Dakota, while inside work goes on all year.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: Every job is different.

  • Morning: Move furniture, lay drop cloths, and tape trim.
  • Later: Patch holes and sand the walls smooth.
  • Midday: Prime the patched spots.
  • Afternoon: Cut in edges with a brush and roll the walls.
  • Before leaving: Clean brushes and rollers and check the work in good light.

Some days are spent high on a ladder outside. Others are quiet indoor work.
How You Learn the Job

Most painters learn on the job. Many employers hire people with a high school diploma or GED, and some do not require one.

  • On-the-job training: An experienced painter teaches prep, tools, and safety.
  • Apprenticeship: Painter apprenticeships pay you while you learn.
  • Safety training: Ladder, scaffold, and respirator training are common.
  • Lead-safe training: Work on homes built before 1978 follows federal lead-safe rules, and the company must be certified. Workers are trained in lead-safe work practices.

Paying for training: In an apprenticeship you are paid while you learn, and pay usually rises as you complete hours. For classes or a certificate, start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. Ask employers whether they help pay. Ask your career counselor about other help, such as WIOA, a federal program that can help some people pay for job training. Ask before you enroll.
Training and Employer Requirements

North Dakota does not license painters. Painting contractors need a state contractor license for larger jobs, and that is the employer’s responsibility. Ask what you need to start.

  • Ability to climb ladders, stand, and reach for long periods, or ask about the physical demands.
  • Comfort wearing a mask or respirator when needed.
  • A driver’s license for travel to job sites.
  • Lead-safe training if the employer works on older homes.

Before you begin: Ask who trains new painters and what safety gear is provided.

Ask about written instructions, a buddy on your first jobs, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and work safely.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota painter pay — May 2025:

  • Middle pay: $26.38 an hour ($54,870 a year). Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $22.75 and $29.16 an hour.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $17.71 an hour, and 1 in 10 earned more than $37.64.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 610 of these jobs in 2024. The state projects about 640 in 2034, a change of +5%. That works out to about 50 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

Where people work: Painting contractors, building contractors, schools and hospitals, property managers, and self-employment.

Work setting: Inside homes and buildings, and outside on ladders and scaffolding. Outdoor work is seasonal.

Compare an offer: Ask about base pay, winter work, overtime, benefits, and what safety gear is provided.
Where This Can Lead

• Experienced painter: Take on spraying, special finishes, or commercial jobs.
  • Crew leader: Lead a painting crew.
  • Estimator: Measure jobs and figure costs.
  • Your own business: Some painters start their own company, which needs a contractor license and insurance.

Ask painters near you which paths are open.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • A clear before and after.
  • Careful, detailed hands-on work.
  • Starting without a degree.
  • Inside work in winter and outside work in summer.

sections: Welcome

Hail, wind, and snow are hard on roofs. Roofers build and repair them so homes and businesses stay dry.

This is physical work at heights, usually outside. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is a Roofer?

You install, repair, and replace roofs on houses and other buildings.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Tear off old roofing and clear the work area.
  • Lay underlayment and waterproofing.
  • Install shingles, metal, or flat-roof systems.
  • Cut and fit shingles and flashing around chimneys and vents.
  • Inspect roofs for damage.
  • Clean up nails and debris.

The real picture: Work depends on the season and the weather. After a hailstorm, crews can be very busy.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: Every crew works differently.

  • Early morning: Set up ladders, anchors, and harnesses before the heat.
  • Morning: Tear off old shingles and load them into a dumpster.
  • Midday: Lay new underlayment and flashing.
  • Afternoon: Nail down new shingles row by row.
  • Before leaving: Clean up nails with a magnet and cover any open areas.

Rain or high wind can stop work for the day.
How You Learn the Job

Most roofers learn on the job. Many employers hire people with a high school diploma or GED, and some do not require one.

  • On-the-job training: An experienced roofer teaches tools, materials, and safe work at heights.
  • Apprenticeship: Roofer apprenticeships pay you while you learn.
  • Fall protection: Training in harnesses, anchors, and ladder safety is part of the job.

Paying for training: In an apprenticeship you are paid while you learn, and pay usually rises as you complete hours. For classes or a certificate, start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. North Dakota does not license individual roofers. Roofing contractors need a state contractor license for jobs over $4,000, with proof of insurance and workers’ compensation coverage. State law also bars roofing contractors from promising to cover a customer’s insurance deductible.

  • Comfort working at heights.
  • Ability to lift and carry heavy bundles, or ask about the physical demands.
  • A driver’s license and a reliable ride to job sites.
  • Fall-protection training, which employers should provide.

What is a Sheet Metal Worker?

You make and install products from thin metal, such as heating and cooling ducts, roof flashing, and gutters.

What is a Butcher and Meat Cutter?

You cut, trim, and package meat so it is ready to sell and cook. You work at grocery store meat counters, local meat markets and locker plants, and processing plants.

Most people learn on the job. Many employers hire people with a high school diploma or GED. Training can take from a few weeks to about a year.

sections: Welcome

Inside every jail and prison, officers keep things safe and running, around the clock. They also shape the daily lives of the people who live there.

This job mixes security, structure, and people skills. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is a Correctional Officer?

You keep order and safety in a jail or prison. You supervise residents, follow security procedures, and respond when something goes wrong.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Supervise residents during daily activities.
  • Count residents and check locks, doors, and gates.
  • Search areas for items that are not allowed.
  • Screen visitors and control entrances.
  • Write reports about incidents and daily activity.
  • Help residents get to programs, meals, and appointments.

The real picture: Most of the job is talking, watching, and following routines. Being fair and consistent prevents many problems.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: Every facility runs on its own schedule.

  • Start of shift: Get a briefing from the officers going off duty.
  • Morning: Do a count and walk a housing unit.
  • Midday: Supervise meals and movement to programs.
  • Afternoon: Watch cameras at a control station and screen visitors.
  • End of shift: Write reports and brief the next shift.

Most shifts are routine, and some are tense. Officers work as a team and call for help when needed.
How You Learn the Job

A high school diploma or GED is what most jobs ask for. The North Dakota Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation says it trains new officers and pays them while they train.

  • Paid training: New officers learn security, communication, first aid, and how to calm tense situations.
  • County jails: North Dakota law requires jail staff who work directly with residents to complete training approved by the state Peace Officer Standards and Training board.
  • Optional education: Minot State University offers a corrections and criminal justice program.

Paying for training:

  1. Start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. The school's financial aid office can help.
  2. Ask employers whether they help pay for training.
  3. Ask for the full cost, including books, fees, travel, and a computer.
  4. Ask your career counselor about other help, such as WIOA. WIOA is a federal program that can help some people pay for job training. Ask before you enroll.

Employer help with school may come with a promise to keep working there. Read the terms first.
Training and Employer Requirements

Requirements depend on the employer. Ask each one what you need.

  • A high school diploma or GED.
  • A minimum age; county jails often require age 18, and some employers require 21.
  • A background check, drug test, and sometimes a physical or fitness test.
  • Completion of the employer’s training program.
  • Willingness to work rotating shifts, including nights and holidays.

Before you begin: Ask how long training lasts and what support new officers get, including help after a hard shift.

Ask about written instructions, an accessible workstation, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and do the work well.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota correctional officer pay — May 2025:

  • Middle pay: $25.22 an hour ($52,460 a year). Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $23.77 and $29.39 an hour.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $22.88 an hour, and 1 in 10 earned more than $30.23.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 1,070 of these jobs in 2024. The state projects about 1,000 in 2034, a change of -6%. That works out to about 90 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

Where people work: State prisons run by the ND Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, county and regional jails, and juvenile facilities.

Work setting: Inside secure facilities, with rotating shifts around the clock.

Compare an offer: Ask about base pay, shift pay, overtime, benefits, retirement, and paid training.
Where This Can Lead

• Senior officer or trainer: Train new staff.
  • Sergeant, lieutenant, or supervisor: Lead a shift.
  • Case manager or programs: Help residents prepare to return to the community.
  • Related careers: Probation officer, police officer, or 911 dispatcher.

Ask officers where you would work which paths are open.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • Paid training and steady public-sector benefits.
  • Clear rules and teamwork.
  • Starting with a high school diploma.
  • A chance to treat people with dignity in a hard place.

Things to ask about:

  • Stress and exposure to conflict.
  • Nights, weekends, holidays, and mandatory overtime.
  • The emotional weight of the work.
  • Support for officers’ mental health.

North Dakota projects about a 6% drop in these jobs from 2024 to 2034, but there are still about 90 openings a year as people retire or change jobs.

A question for yourself: Can you see yourself staying calm, fair, and steady in a structured, sometimes tense place?

sections: Welcome

When someone decides to change their relationship with alcohol or drugs, a counselor is often part of that journey.

This career mixes listening, planning, and hope. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is a Substance Abuse Counselor?

You help people who struggle with alcohol, drugs, or other addictive behaviors. You meet with people one-on-one and in groups, and you work with their families and other providers.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Meet with clients to understand their needs and goals.
  • Write treatment plans with each person.
  • Lead individual and group sessions.
  • Track progress and adjust plans.
  • Work with doctors, nurses, social workers, and courts.
  • Step in to help when someone is in crisis.

The real picture: Recovery is rarely a straight line. Counselors celebrate progress and keep going through setbacks.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: Every program works differently.

  • Morning: Review notes and meet with the team about new clients.
  • Later: Meet one-on-one with two clients.
  • Midday: Lead a group session.
  • Afternoon: Update treatment plans and call a client’s doctor.
  • Before leaving: Finish notes and plan tomorrow.

Some days are hopeful and others are heavy. Supervision and teamwork help counselors keep going.
How You Learn the Job

This career takes college and a state license. North Dakota licensed addiction counselors complete board-approved college coursework, at least 960 hours of supervised clinical training, and a national exam.

  • North Dakota programs: Minot State University and the University of Mary offer bachelor’s programs in addiction counseling. Nueta Hidatsa Sahnish College in New Town offers an associate program.
  • Clinical training: You practice under supervision in an approved program.
  • Another route: Licensed professional counselors in North Dakota need a master’s degree in counseling; some also treat addiction.
  • Start nearby: Recovery support, peer support, or human service assistant jobs can be a first step.

Paying for training:

  1. Start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. The school's financial aid office can help.
  2. Ask employers whether they help pay for training.
  3. Ask for the full cost, including books, fees, travel, and a computer.
  4. Ask your career counselor about other help, such as WIOA. WIOA is a federal program that can help some people pay for job training. Ask before you enroll.

Employer help with school may come with a promise to keep working there. Read the terms first.
Training and Employer Requirements

To practice as a licensed addiction counselor in North Dakota, you need a license from the North Dakota Board of Addiction Counseling Examiners. Confirm the exact education rules with the board before you choose a program.

  • Board-approved college coursework.
  • At least 960 hours of supervised clinical training.
  • Passing the board-approved exam.
  • A background check for most jobs.
  • Continuing education to keep the license.

Before you begin: Ask schools how they help students find clinical training placements.

Ask about written instructions, an accessible workstation, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and do the work well.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota substance abuse counselor pay — May 2025:

  • Middle pay: $33.00 an hour ($68,630 a year). Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $26.66 and $37.17 an hour.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $20.80 an hour, and 1 in 10 earned more than $41.65.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 1,260 of these jobs in 2024. The state projects about 1,500 in 2034, a change of +20%. That works out to about 130 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

Where people work: Treatment centers, hospitals, human service centers, tribal health programs, correctional facilities, and private practices.

Work setting: Offices and group rooms, sometimes with evening hours. Some counselors work by video.

Compare an offer: Ask about base pay, supervision for your license, caseload size, benefits, and help with continuing education.
Where This Can Lead

• Experienced counselor: Specialize in youth, families, or co-occurring mental health needs.
  • Clinical supervisor: Train and supervise new counselors.
  • Program director: Lead a treatment program.
  • More education: A master’s degree can lead to a professional counselor license.

Ask counselors near you which paths are open.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • Helping people rebuild their lives.
  • Strong demand in North Dakota.
  • A licensed profession with room to grow.
  • Teamwork with other helpers.

Things to ask about:

  • Emotional weight and burnout.
  • Lots of paperwork.
  • Clients who relapse or stop coming.
  • Years of school and training before full licensure.

North Dakota projects about 20% growth in these jobs from 2024 to 2034, with about 130 openings a year.

What is a Psychiatric Technician?

You care for people who are getting treatment for mental illness or developmental disabilities. You work under nurses and doctors as part of a team.

sections: Welcome

Sometimes the most helpful health worker is someone from the neighborhood who knows how to explain things and where to find help.

This job mixes outreach, education, and support. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is a Community Health Worker?

You help people understand their health and connect with care and services. You often work in the community you come from.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Visit people at home or meet them in the community.
  • Explain health information in plain words.
  • Help people manage conditions like diabetes day to day.
  • Connect people with clinics and services.
  • Follow up to see how things are going.
  • Keep records of visits.

The real picture: Titles vary, such as community health representative, outreach worker, or patient navigator.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: Every program works differently.

  • Morning: Plan home visits and check messages.
  • Later: Visit a client to talk about managing blood sugar.
  • Midday: Help another client schedule a clinic visit and find a ride.
  • Afternoon: Staff a table at a community event.
  • Before leaving: Record visits and plan follow-ups.

Much of the day is spent on the road and with people, not at a desk.
How You Learn the Job

North Dakota began certifying community health workers in October 2025. Certification creates a way for North Dakota Medicaid to pay for their services.

  • Certification pathways: A CHW training program plus a 200-hour internship; Indian Health Service community health representative training; 1,000 hours of supervised CHW work within three years; or certification from another state.
  • College: Some employers want a degree in public health or a related field. North Dakota options include UND, NDSU, Dickinson State University, the University of Jamestown, and Turtle Mountain College.
  • On-the-job training: Employers teach their programs and community resources.

Paying for training:

  1. Start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. The school's financial aid office can help.
  2. Ask employers whether they help pay for training.
  3. Ask for the full cost, including books, fees, travel, and a computer.
  4. Ask your career counselor about other help, such as WIOA. WIOA is a federal program that can help some people pay for job training. Ask before you enroll.

Employer help with school may come with a promise to keep working there. Read the terms first.
Training and Employer Requirements

Ask each employer whether they require North Dakota CHW certification. Certified CHWs renew with 12 hours of continuing education, including 2 on legal and ethical topics.

  • Strong ties to the community you will serve.
  • A driver’s license and reliable car for visits.
  • A background check.
  • Comfort keeping health information private.

Before you begin: Ask how the employer trains and supervises CHWs.

Ask about written instructions, an accessible workstation, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and do the work well.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota community health worker pay — May 2025:

  • Middle pay: $28.66 an hour ($59,610 a year). Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $22.18 and $35.33 an hour.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $21.54 an hour, and 1 in 10 earned more than $36.64.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 90 of these jobs in 2024. The state projects about 100 in 2034, a change of +10%. That works out to about 10 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

Where people work: Public health units, clinics and hospitals, tribal health programs, and nonprofits.

Work setting: Homes, community places, and offices, with a lot of driving.

Compare an offer: Ask about base pay, mileage, whether the job is grant funded, benefits, and training.
Where This Can Lead

• Senior CHW or team lead: Train and support new CHWs.
  • Health educator: With more education.
  • Nursing or social work: Many CHWs go on to college.
  • Program coordinator: Run a community health program.

Ask people in public health near you which paths are open.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • Helping your own community.
  • Time out with people instead of at a desk.
  • A growing field with new certification.
  • Seeing people get healthier.

Things to ask about:

  • Few jobs in some areas.
  • Travel and mileage.
  • Jobs that depend on grant funding.
  • The emotional weight of people’s struggles.

North Dakota projects about 10% growth in these jobs from 2024 to 2034. It is a small field, with about 10 openings a year.

A question for yourself: Would you like to be the trusted person who helps neighbors find care?

sections: Welcome

The first voice people hear in an emergency belongs to a 911 dispatcher.

This job mixes calm communication, quick thinking, and teamwork. Explore what it feels like before deciding whether it interests you.

Go at your pace. The short questions at the end are for reflection. There are no right or wrong answers.
What is a 911 Dispatcher?

You answer emergency and non-emergency calls and send police, fire, and ambulance crews where they are needed.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Answer calls and find out where the caller is.
  • Ask questions to learn what is happening.
  • Decide which calls are most urgent.
  • Send the right crews by radio and computer.
  • Give callers instructions until help arrives.
  • Record details of every call.

The real picture: Many calls are not emergencies. Some are frightening. Dispatchers handle both, often at the same time.
A Day in the Life

{{IMAGE1}}

One possible day: Every center is different.

  • Start of shift: Get a briefing on what is happening in the area.
  • Morning: Handle a car crash call and send crews.
  • Midday: Answer non-emergency calls and track units by radio.
  • Afternoon: Give a caller medical instructions until the ambulance arrives.
  • End of shift: Finish records and brief the next dispatcher.

Quiet stretches can change in seconds.
How You Learn the Job

Most centers hire people with a high school diploma or GED and train them.

  • Required training: North Dakota law requires each 911 center to give dispatchers initial and ongoing training.
  • Medical instructions: Dispatchers who give medical instructions before help arrives must finish an approved emergency medical dispatch course.
  • On the job: New dispatchers train with an experienced dispatcher before working alone.

Paying for training:

  1. Start with financial aid, scholarships, and grants. The school's financial aid office can help.
  2. Ask employers whether they help pay for training.
  3. Ask for the full cost, including books, fees, travel, and a computer.
  4. Ask your career counselor about other help, such as WIOA. WIOA is a federal program that can help some people pay for job training. Ask before you enroll.

Employer help with school may come with a promise to keep working there. Read the terms first.
Training and Employer Requirements

North Dakota sets hiring rules for 911 centers. Ask each center for its full list.

  • Fingerprinting and a nationwide background check, with no felony conviction.
  • Drug screening and a hearing test before hiring.
  • Initial and ongoing training from the center.
  • An emergency medical dispatch course to give medical instructions.
  • Willingness to work rotating 24/7 shifts.

Before you begin: Ask how the center supports dispatchers after hard calls.

Ask about written instructions, an accessible workstation, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and do the work well.
Pay and Job Outlook

North Dakota 911 dispatcher pay — May 2025:

  • Middle pay: $28.82 an hour ($59,940 a year). Half of workers earned more and half earned less.
  • Half of workers earned between $23.88 and $29.45 an hour.
  • 1 in 10 earned less than $22.97 an hour, and 1 in 10 earned more than $30.37.
  • These numbers show what workers earned. They are not a promise of what a new worker will start at.
  • North Dakota had about 300 of these jobs in 2024. The state projects about 320 in 2034, a change of +6%. That works out to about 30 openings a year, mostly from people who retire or change jobs.

Where people work: City and county 911 centers, state radio, and some hospitals and ambulance services.

Work setting: Dispatch centers with computers and radios, staffed 24 hours a day.

Compare an offer: Ask about base pay, shift pay, overtime, benefits, and support after hard calls.
Where This Can Lead

• Senior dispatcher or trainer: Train new dispatchers.
  • Shift supervisor: Lead a team.
  • 911 center manager: Run a dispatch center.
  • Related careers: EMT, firefighter, or police officer.

Ask dispatchers near you which paths are open.
The Real Talk

Things you might like:

  • Helping people at the most important moment.
  • Teamwork with first responders.
  • Paid training and steady public jobs.
  • Fast-paced, never-boring work.

Things to ask about:

  • Stress and upsetting calls.
  • Nights, weekends, holidays, and overtime.
  • Long shifts at a console.
  • Support for dispatchers’ mental health.

North Dakota projects about 6% growth in these jobs from 2024 to 2034, with about 30 openings a year.

A question for yourself: Can you stay calm and clear when someone else is in crisis?

What is a Recreation Worker?

You plan and lead activities like sports, games, crafts, and fitness classes in parks, camps, and community centers.

{{IMAGE0}}
  • Set up equipment and spaces.
  • Lead games, sports, crafts, and classes.
  • Plan activities that fit each group.
  • Enforce safety rules.
  • Give first aid when needed.
  • Keep attendance and supply records.

The real picture: Many jobs are part time or seasonal. Full-time jobs often involve more planning and leadership.

One possible day: Every program is different.

  • Morning: Set up the field for a youth soccer program.
  • Later: Lead drills and games.
  • Midday: Lead a chair exercise class at the senior center.
  • Afternoon: Plan next week’s activities.
  • Before leaving: Put away equipment and write down attendance.

Weather and turnout can change the plan.

Many part-time jobs need only a high school diploma, and some take teens. Full-time jobs often want a college degree in recreation or a related field.

  • On-the-job training: Employers teach their programs and safety rules.
  • Certifications: CPR and first aid are common. Pool jobs need lifeguard certification.
  • Start nearby: Volunteering or summer camp jobs build experience.

  • A background check for work with children or vulnerable adults.
  • Ability to be active and on your feet.
  • Willingness to work evenings, weekends, or summers.

Before you begin: Ask what training is provided and how staff handle emergencies.

Ask about written instructions, an accessible workstation, extra practice time, or other support that helps you learn and do the work well.

Where people work: Park districts, cities, YMCAs, camps, senior centers, nursing homes, and after-school programs.

Compare an offer: Ask about hourly pay, hours per week, season length, and whether full-time work is available.

• Program leader: Plan and run whole programs.
